problems.problem_statement: Find the general solution to the differential equation \\( \\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{x^2}{y} \\).
problems.solution: The given differential equation is \\( \\frac{dy}{dx} = \\frac{x^2}{y} \\). This is a separable equation. We can separate the variables by multiplying both sides by \\(y\\) and \\(dx\\): \\( y \\, dy = x^2 \\, dx \\). Next, we integrate both sides: \\( \\int y \\, dy = \\int x^2 \\, dx \\). Performing the integration gives: \\( \\frac{y^2}{2} = \\frac{x^3}{3} + C_1 \\), where \\(C_1\\) is the constant of integration. To eliminate the fractions, we can multiply the entire equation by 6: \\( 3y^2 = 2x^3 + 6C_1 \\). Let \\(C = 6C_1\\). Since \\(C_1\\) is an arbitrary constant, \\(C\\) is also an arbitrary constant. Rearranging the terms, we get the general solution in implicit form: \\( 3y^2 - 2x^3 = C \\).

scaffolding.hint: The given differential equation is of the form \\( \\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)g(y) \\). Identify \\(f(x)\\) and \\(g(y)\\) and rearrange the equation to group all \\(y\\) terms with \\(dy\\) and all \\(x\\) terms with \\(dx\\).

After separating the variables, you should have an equation of the form \\( h(y) dy = k(x) dx \\). Integrate both sides with respect to their respective variables: \\( \\int h(y) dy = \\int k(x) dx \\). Remember the power rule for integration: \\( \\int u^n du = \\frac{u^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \\).

The integration will result in an equation involving \\(y^2\\) and \\(x^3\\), plus a constant of integration. Combine the constants into a single arbitrary constant \\(C\\) and rearrange the terms to match one of the given options.
